intuition:
Imagine two hiking trails running side by side on a mountain — one always a little higher than the other. To find how much extra ground lies between them, you slice the strip into many thin vertical bands, measure the height of each band (the gap between the trails), and add them all up. That is exactly what the area (넓이) between two curves (곡선) means in calculus: the region (영역) trapped between $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ over an interval $[a,b]$, built from infinitely many infinitesimally thin rectangles.

💡 The area between two curves on $[a,b]$ is the definite integral (정적분) of (top curve − bottom curve), and you must always check which curve is actually on top before integrating.
definition:
Formally, if a curve $y=f(x)$ lies above the x-axis (x축) on $[a,b]$ — meaning $f(x)\ge 0$ there — the area between the curve and the x-axis is simply

$$A=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

🗣 "A equals the integral from a to b of f of x, d x."

If instead the curve dips below the x-axis somewhere on $[a,b]$, a plain integral would let the negative part cancel the positive part, so you must use the absolute value (절댓값) of $f$, splitting the integral at every point where $f(x)=0$:

$$A=\int_a^b |f(x)|\,dx,$$

🗣 "A equals the integral from a to b of the absolute value of f of x, d x, computed by splitting at each zero and adding the pieces as positive amounts."

The same idea extends to the region between two curves. If $f(x)\ge g(x)$ for every $x$ in $[a,b]$ — that is, $f$ stays on top the whole way — then

$$A=\int_a^b \big(f(x)-g(x)\big)\,dx.$$

🗣 "A equals the integral from a to b of f of x minus g of x, d x."

If the two curves cross inside $[a,b]$, find every intersection point (교점) first by solving $f(x)=g(x)$, then split the integral at those points and always subtract the lower curve from the upper curve on each piece.
workedExample:
Find the area of the region enclosed between $f(x)=8-x^2$ and $g(x)=x^2$.

Step 1 — Find where the curves intersect by setting $f(x)=g(x)$:

$$8-x^2=x^2 \;\Longrightarrow\; 2x^2=8 \;\Longrightarrow\; x^2=4 \;\Longrightarrow\; x=-2,\ 2.$$

🗣 "Eight minus x squared equals x squared gives x equals negative two or two."

So the enclosed region runs from $x=-2$ to $x=2$.

Step 2 — Decide which curve is on top by testing a point inside the interval, say $x=0$: $f(0)=8$ and $g(0)=0$, so $f(x)\ge g(x)$ on $[-2,2]$ — the downward-opening parabola $f$ sits above $g$ the whole way.

Step 3 — Set up the integral of (top − bottom) and find the antiderivative (부정적분):

$$A=\int_{-2}^{2}\big[(8-x^2)-x^2\big]\,dx=\int_{-2}^{2}(8-2x^2)\,dx=\Big[8x-\tfrac{2x^3}{3}\Big]_{-2}^{2}.$$

🗣 "A equals the integral from negative two to two of eight minus two x squared, d x."

Step 4 — Evaluate at both endpoints and subtract.

At $x=2$: $8(2)-\tfrac{2(2)^3}{3}=16-\tfrac{16}{3}=\tfrac{32}{3}$.

At $x=-2$: $8(-2)-\tfrac{2(-2)^3}{3}=-16+\tfrac{16}{3}=-\tfrac{32}{3}$.

$$A=\frac{32}{3}-\left(-\frac{32}{3}\right)=\frac{64}{3}.$$

🗣 "A equals thirty-two thirds minus negative thirty-two thirds, which is sixty-four thirds."

So the area enclosed between the two parabolas is $\dfrac{64}{3}$ square units.
teachingNote: A very common mistake is integrating $f(x)-g(x)$ without first checking which function is actually larger on the interval, which can produce a negative number that students then just report as the 'area' — or worse, cancel out entirely when the difference changes sign. Always find the intersection points first, test one sample x-value to see which curve is on top, and if the sign of $f(x)-g(x)$ changes anywhere inside $[a,b]$, split the integral at that point and take the absolute value of each piece before adding — the same rule that applies to a single curve dipping below the x-axis.
note:
📌 Note: The area (넓이) between $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ on $[a,b]$ is one number measuring how much region is trapped between the two curves (곡선), always found by integrating the top function minus the bottom function — never the reverse. Key formulas: $A=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ for a curve above the x-axis (x축); $A=\int_a^b |f(x)|\,dx$, splitting at each root, when it dips below; and $A=\int_a^b (f(x)-g(x))\,dx$ with $f(x)\ge g(x)$ for the region between two curves, splitting at every intersection point (교점) if they cross.

🗣 "A equals the integral from a to b of f of x minus g of x, d x, whenever f is on top."

Terms introduced in this lesson: area (넓이), curve (곡선), x-axis (x축), region (영역), absolute value (절댓값), definite integral (정적분), antiderivative (부정적분), and intersection point (교점).

practice.prompt: Find the area between the curve $y=x^2$ and the x-axis on the interval $[0,3]$.
practice.solution:
Since $y=x^2\ge 0$ on $[0,3]$, the area is just the plain definite integral:

$$A=\int_0^3 x^2\,dx=\Big[\tfrac{x^3}{3}\Big]_0^3=\frac{27}{3}-0=9.$$

🗣 "A equals the integral from zero to three of x squared, d x, which equals nine."

practice.prompt: Find the area of the region enclosed between $f(x)=x+4$ and $g(x)=x^2-2$.
practice.solution:
Step 1 — Find the intersection points by setting $f(x)=g(x)$:

$$x+4=x^2-2 \;\Longrightarrow\; x^2-x-6=0 \;\Longrightarrow\; (x-3)(x+2)=0 \;\Longrightarrow\; x=-2,\ 3.$$

🗣 "x squared minus x minus six equals zero factors to x equals negative two or three."

Step 2 — Test $x=0$: $f(0)=4$ and $g(0)=-2$, so $f(x)\ge g(x)$ on $[-2,3]$ — the line stays above the parabola.

Step 3 — Integrate (top − bottom) and evaluate:

$$A=\int_{-2}^{3}\big[(x+4)-(x^2-2)\big]\,dx=\int_{-2}^{3}(6+x-x^2)\,dx=\Big[6x+\tfrac{x^2}{2}-\tfrac{x^3}{3}\Big]_{-2}^{3}.$$

🗣 "A equals the integral from negative two to three of six plus x minus x squared, d x."

At $x=3$: $18+4.5-9=13.5=\tfrac{27}{2}$. At $x=-2$: $-12+2+\tfrac{8}{3}=-\tfrac{22}{3}$.

$$A=\frac{27}{2}-\left(-\frac{22}{3}\right)=\frac{81}{6}+\frac{44}{6}=\frac{125}{6}.$$

🗣 "A equals twenty-seven halves plus twenty-two thirds, which equals one hundred twenty-five sixths."

practice.prompt: Find the area between the curve $f(x)=x^2-4$ and the x-axis on $[-1,3]$. (The curve dips below the x-axis on part of this interval, so split the integral.)
practice.solution:
Step 1 — Find where $f(x)=0$ inside the interval: $x^2-4=0 \Rightarrow x=\pm2$. Only $x=2$ lies in $[-1,3]$, so the curve is negative on $[-1,2]$ and positive on $[2,3]$.

🗣 "f of x equals zero at x equals negative two or two, and only two is inside negative one to three."

Step 2 — On $[-1,2]$, $f(x)\le 0$, so integrate $-f(x)$:

$$\int_{-1}^{2} -(x^2-4)\,dx=\int_{-1}^{2}(4-x^2)\,dx=\Big[4x-\tfrac{x^3}{3}\Big]_{-1}^{2}=\frac{16}{3}-\left(-\frac{11}{3}\right)=9.$$

🗣 "The integral of four minus x squared from negative one to two equals nine."

Step 3 — On $[2,3]$, $f(x)\ge 0$, so integrate $f(x)$ directly:

$$\int_{2}^{3}(x^2-4)\,dx=\Big[\tfrac{x^3}{3}-4x\Big]_{2}^{3}=-3-\left(-\frac{16}{3}\right)=\frac{7}{3}.$$

🗣 "The integral of x squared minus four from two to three equals seven thirds."

Step 4 — Add the two pieces:

$$A=9+\frac{7}{3}=\frac{27}{3}+\frac{7}{3}=\frac{34}{3}.$$

🗣 "A equals nine plus seven thirds, which is thirty-four thirds."

quiz.prompt: Find the area between the curve $y=3x^2$ and the x-axis on $[0,2]$.
quiz.solution:
Since $y=3x^2\ge0$ on $[0,2]$, integrate directly:

$$A=\int_0^2 3x^2\,dx=\Big[x^3\Big]_0^2=8-0=8.$$

🗣 "A equals the integral from zero to two of three x squared, d x, which equals eight."

quiz.prompt: Find the area of the region enclosed between $f(x)=2x+3$ and $g(x)=x^2$.
quiz.solution:
Step 1 — Find the intersection points: $2x+3=x^2 \Rightarrow x^2-2x-3=0 \Rightarrow (x-3)(x+1)=0 \Rightarrow x=-1,\ 3$.

🗣 "x squared minus two x minus three equals zero factors to x equals negative one or three."

Step 2 — Test $x=0$: $f(0)=3$ and $g(0)=0$, so $f(x)\ge g(x)$ on $[-1,3]$.

Step 3 — Integrate (top − bottom):

$$A=\int_{-1}^{3}\big[(2x+3)-x^2\big]\,dx=\int_{-1}^{3}(-x^2+2x+3)\,dx=\Big[-\tfrac{x^3}{3}+x^2+3x\Big]_{-1}^{3}.$$

🗣 "A equals the integral from negative one to three of negative x squared plus two x plus three, d x."

At $x=3$: $-9+9+9=9$. At $x=-1$: $\tfrac{1}{3}+1-3=-\tfrac{5}{3}$.

$$A=9-\left(-\frac{5}{3}\right)=\frac{27}{3}+\frac{5}{3}=\frac{32}{3}.$$

🗣 "A equals nine plus five thirds, which equals thirty-two thirds."

quiz.prompt: Find the area between the curve $f(x)=x^2-9$ and the x-axis on $[-2,4]$. (The curve dips below the x-axis on part of this interval, so split the integral.)
quiz.solution:
Step 1 — Find where $f(x)=0$ inside the interval: $x^2-9=0 \Rightarrow x=\pm3$. Only $x=3$ lies in $[-2,4]$, so $f(x)\le0$ on $[-2,3]$ and $f(x)\ge0$ on $[3,4]$.

🗣 "f of x equals zero at x equals negative three or three, and only three is inside negative two to four."

Step 2 — On $[-2,3]$, integrate $-f(x)$:

$$\int_{-2}^{3}(9-x^2)\,dx=\Big[9x-\tfrac{x^3}{3}\Big]_{-2}^{3}=18-\left(-\frac{46}{3}\right)=\frac{100}{3}.$$

🗣 "The integral of nine minus x squared from negative two to three equals one hundred thirds."

Step 3 — On $[3,4]$, integrate $f(x)$ directly:

$$\int_{3}^{4}(x^2-9)\,dx=\Big[\tfrac{x^3}{3}-9x\Big]_{3}^{4}=-\frac{44}{3}-\left(-\frac{54}{3}\right)=\frac{10}{3}.$$

🗣 "The integral of x squared minus nine from three to four equals ten thirds."

Step 4 — Add the two pieces:

$$A=\frac{100}{3}+\frac{10}{3}=\frac{110}{3}.$$

🗣 "A equals one hundred thirds plus ten thirds, which is one hundred ten thirds."

goingDeeper:
A trickier situation arises when the two curves cross each other more than twice on the interval, so the difference $f(x)-g(x)$ changes sign (부호가 바뀜) more than once — you then need more than one split point.

Step 1 — Let $f(x)=x^3-3x$ and $g(x)=x$, and find every intersection point (교점) by solving $f(x)=g(x)$.

$$x^3-3x=x \;\Longrightarrow\; x^3-4x=0 \;\Longrightarrow\; x(x-2)(x+2)=0 \;\Longrightarrow\; x=-2,\,0,\,2.$$

🗣 "x cubed minus three x equals x gives x times x minus two times x plus two equals zero, so x equals negative two, zero, or two."

Step 2 — Because there are three intersection points, check the sign of $h(x)=f(x)-g(x)=x^3-4x$ separately on $(-2,0)$ and $(0,2)$ by testing one value in each.

At $x=-1$: $h(-1)=(-1)^3-4(-1)=3>0$, so $f$ is on top on $(-2,0)$. At $x=1$: $h(1)=1-4=-3<0$, so $g$ is on top on $(0,2)$ — the curves swap places at $x=0$.

Step 3 — Set up two separate integrals, always subtracting the lower curve from the upper curve on each piece.

$$A=\int_{-2}^{0}\big[(x^3-3x)-x\big]\,dx+\int_{0}^{2}\big[x-(x^3-3x)\big]\,dx=\int_{-2}^{0}(x^3-4x)\,dx+\int_{0}^{2}(4x-x^3)\,dx.$$

🗣 "A equals the integral from negative two to zero of x cubed minus four x, d x, plus the integral from zero to two of four x minus x cubed, d x."

Step 4 — Find the antiderivative $\frac{x^4}{4}-2x^2$ for the first piece and evaluate.

$$\Big[\frac{x^4}{4}-2x^2\Big]_{-2}^{0}=0-(4-8)=4.$$

Step 5 — Find the antiderivative $2x^2-\frac{x^4}{4}$ for the second piece and evaluate.

$$\Big[2x^2-\frac{x^4}{4}\Big]_{0}^{2}=(8-4)-0=4.$$

Adding the two pieces gives $A=4+4=8$ square units — notice that even though the two curves bound a 'crossing' shape rather than a single simple lens, the same split-and-absolute-value logic from the single-curve case still applies, just to $f(x)-g(x)$ instead of to $f(x)$ alone.

{{graph:cubic-line-crossing}}

❌ A common shortcut is to integrate $f(x)-g(x)$ across the whole interval in one go, i.e. computing $\int_{-2}^{2}(x^3-4x)\,dx$ without splitting at $x=0$.

✅ Because $h(x)=x^3-4x$ is an odd function (홀함수), that single integral evaluates to exactly $0$ — the positive region above and the negative region below cancel perfectly, even though the actual enclosed area is $8$, not $0$. Always split at every interior zero of $f(x)-g(x)$ before adding.

❌ Another frequent error is finding the intersection points correctly but then testing the sign of $f(x)-g(x)$ only once for the whole interval, assuming that because the curves crossed at one point they can't cross again elsewhere.

✅ Every root of $f(x)=g(x)$ is a candidate split point; test a sample value inside each subinterval formed by consecutive roots, since a cubic (or higher-degree) difference can flip sign multiple times.

Edge cases are worth flagging too. If $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ merely touch at a point without crossing — for instance when $f(x)-g(x)$ has a double root (중근), like $h(x)=x^2(x-1)$ — the sign of $h$ does not actually flip there, since $x^2\ge 0$ regardless of sign; in that case you do NOT need to split the integral at that touching point, only at points where the sign genuinely changes. And if $a=b$ (a degenerate interval of zero width), the area is trivially $0$, since a definite integral over a single point contributes nothing.

advanced.content:
Consider the curve $f(x)=|x^2-4|$ and the horizontal line $g(x)=5$. Find the area of the region enclosed between the curve and the line.

Step 1 — Express $f$ piecewise, since the absolute value (절댓값) splits its formula depending on the sign of $x^2-4$: for $|x|\ge 2$, $f(x)=x^2-4$; for $|x|<2$, $f(x)=4-x^2$.

Step 2 — Find where $f(x)=g(x)=5$. On $|x|<2$, solving $4-x^2=5$ gives $x^2=-1$, which has no real solution, so the curve never reaches height $5$ on that middle piece. On $|x|\ge 2$, solving $x^2-4=5$ gives $x^2=9$, so $x=\pm 3$.

$$x=-3,\ 3.$$

🗣 "x squared minus four equals five gives x equals negative three or three."

Step 3 — Confirm the line stays above the curve for the entire interval $[-3,3]$: on $[-2,2]$, $f(x)=4-x^2\le 4<5$; on $[2,3]$ and $[-3,-2]$, $f(x)=x^2-4$ rises from $0$ up to exactly $5$ at $x=\pm3$. So $g(x)\ge f(x)$ throughout, with equality only at the two endpoints — no sign change to worry about.

Step 4 — Use the even symmetry (대칭) of $f$ to halve the work: compute the area on $[0,3]$ and double it.

$$A=2\int_{0}^{3}\big(5-f(x)\big)\,dx=2\left[\int_{0}^{2}\big(1+x^2\big)\,dx+\int_{2}^{3}\big(9-x^2\big)\,dx\right].$$

🗣 "A equals two times the integral from zero to two of one plus x squared, d x, plus the integral from two to three of nine minus x squared, d x."

Step 5 — Evaluate each antiderivative.

$$\int_{0}^{2}(1+x^2)\,dx=\Big[x+\frac{x^3}{3}\Big]_{0}^{2}=2+\frac{8}{3}=\frac{14}{3}.$$

$$\int_{2}^{3}(9-x^2)\,dx=\Big[9x-\frac{x^3}{3}\Big]_{2}^{3}=18-\frac{46}{3}=\frac{8}{3}.$$

Step 6 — Add the two pieces and double the total.

$$A=2\left(\frac{14}{3}+\frac{8}{3}\right)=2\cdot\frac{22}{3}=\frac{44}{3}.$$

🗣 "A equals two times twenty-two thirds, which is forty-four thirds."

So the enclosed area is $\dfrac{44}{3}$ square units.

{{graph:abs-parabola-line}}

A curious student might ask why splitting at the zeros of $f(x)-g(x)$ is always mathematically safe — why can't the sign flip again between two consecutive zeros without another root appearing? The reason traces back to continuity (연속성) and the Intermediate Value Theorem (사잇값 정리): if $h(x)=f(x)-g(x)$ is continuous and $h(x)\ne 0$ anywhere strictly between two consecutive roots, then $h$ cannot cross zero there, so by the Intermediate Value Theorem it must keep the same sign on that whole open subinterval — a single test point is therefore enough to characterize the entire piece. This is also why the 'area vs. signed integral' distinction mirrors the classic physics contrast between distance (거리) traveled and displacement (변위): integrating $f(x)-g(x)$ directly gives the net signed quantity (like displacement, where opposite directions cancel), while summing $|f(x)-g(x)|$ piece by piece over each constant-sign interval gives the true total area (like total distance, where every bit of motion counts positively).

practice.prompt: Find the area enclosed between the curve $f(x)=x^3-9x$ and the x-axis on the interval $[-3,3]$. (The curve crosses the x-axis twice inside the interval, so split the integral into three pieces.)
practice.solution:
Step 1 — Solve $x^3-9x=0 \Rightarrow x(x-3)(x+3)=0$, giving zeros at $x=-3,0,3$, which splits $[-3,3]$ into two pieces.

Step 2 — Test signs: at $x=-1$, $f(-1)=-1+9=8>0$; at $x=1$, $f(1)=1-9=-8<0$. So $f\ge0$ on $[-3,0]$ and $f\le0$ on $[0,3]$.

Step 3 — Use the antiderivative $F(x)=\frac{x^4}{4}-\frac{9x^2}{2}$.

$$\int_{-3}^{0}(x^3-9x)\,dx=F(0)-F(-3)=0-\left(\frac{81}{4}-\frac{81}{2}\right)=\frac{81}{4}.$$

$$\int_{0}^{3}(x^3-9x)\,dx=F(3)-F(0)=\left(\frac{81}{4}-\frac{81}{2}\right)-0=-\frac{81}{4}.$$

Step 4 — Take the absolute value of the negative piece and add both pieces: $A=\frac{81}{4}+\frac{81}{4}=\frac{81}{2}$.

practice.prompt: Find the area of the region enclosed between $f(x)=x^3-2x$ and $g(x)=x^2-2x$ on $[-1,2]$. (Note: the curves touch without crossing at one of the intersection points — check whether you actually need to split there.)
practice.solution:
Step 1 — Solve $f(x)=g(x)$: $x^3-2x=x^2-2x \Rightarrow x^3-x^2=0 \Rightarrow x^2(x-1)=0$, giving $x=0$ (a double root) and $x=1$.

Step 2 — Because $x=0$ is a double root, $h(x)=f(x)-g(x)=x^2(x-1)$ does not change sign there, since $x^2\ge0$ always — only $(x-1)$ controls the sign. Testing $x=-1$: $h(-1)=1\cdot(-2)=-2<0$, so $g\ge f$ on $[-1,1]$. Testing $x=2$: $h(2)=4\cdot1=4>0$, so $f\ge g$ on $[1,2]$. Only $x=1$ is an actual split point.

Step 3 — Evaluate each integral.

$$\int_{-1}^{1}(x^2-x^3)\,dx=\Big[\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{x^4}{4}\Big]_{-1}^{1}=\frac{1}{12}-\left(-\frac{7}{12}\right)=\frac{2}{3}.$$

$$\int_{1}^{2}(x^3-x^2)\,dx=\Big[\frac{x^4}{4}-\frac{x^3}{3}\Big]_{1}^{2}=\frac{4}{3}-\left(-\frac{1}{12}\right)=\frac{17}{12}.$$

Step 4 — Add the pieces: $A=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{17}{12}=\frac{8}{12}+\frac{17}{12}=\frac{25}{12}$.
